MCB 1.05 • Explanation-Focused Reviewer

Pathogenesis of Bacterial Infections

Lecture-supported explanations • July 8, 2026 • Version 1

How bacteria move from presence to disease

The lecture organizes pathogenesis as a chain: establish that a microorganism causes disease, understand how it reaches the host, then follow the bacterial traits that permit attachment, invasion, injury, spread, immune evasion, and protein delivery.

PDF pp. 1–9
Central Question
What allows a bacterium to cause infection and disease rather than merely exist in an environment or host? The answer is a coordinated set of virulence factors, many of which are carried or moved by bacterial genetic elements.
1. Establish causeKoch’s postulates and molecular approaches connect an organism or gene to disease.
2. Reach the hostEnvironmental, animal, and human sources create opportunities for transmission.
3. Acquire traitsPlasmids, transposons, phages, and pathogenicity islands carry virulence genes.
4. Act on the hostAdherence, invasion, toxins, enzymes, and secretion systems produce infection.
5. PersistCapsules, intracellular survival, and antigenic variation help bacteria evade defenses.

The main virulence framework

  • Adherence factors — keep bacteria on host surfaces.
  • Invasion — permits entry into host cells and tissues.
  • Toxins — directly alter or injure host cells.
  • Enzymes — facilitate tissue spread or antibody inactivation.
  • Antiphagocytic factors — protect against phagocytic cells.
  • Intracellular pathogenicity — enables survival inside host cells.
  • Antigenic heterogeneity — changes what the immune system sees.
  • Secretion systems — move bacterial proteins or other substrates.

How the topics connect

Genetics supplies the tools. Mobile genetic elements and pathogenicity islands may encode toxins, capsules, adherence factors, invasion products, or antibiotic resistance.

Virulence factors use those tools. Adherence begins colonization; invasion and enzymes open access; toxins create host effects; immune-evasion mechanisms preserve bacterial survival.

Secretion systems deliver many of the tools. The lecture’s final section shows how different bacterial species export proteins involved in pathogenesis.

Establishing cause and tracing transmission

Before discussing virulence, the lecture first asks how we know a bacterium causes a disease and how that bacterium reaches another host.

PDF pp. 1, 9

Koch’s postulates

Simple idea: connect a specific microorganism to a reproducible disease.

  1. The microorganism should be found in all cases of the disease, with its distribution matching the lesions.
  2. It should be grown in pure culture in vitro for several generations.
  3. The pure culture should cause the typical disease when inoculated into a susceptible animal species.
  4. The microorganism should be re-isolated from the experimentally produced lesions.

Molecular Koch’s postulates

Simple idea: instead of proving that the whole organism causes disease, link a specific gene or phenotype to pathogenicity.

  1. The phenotype should be significantly associated with pathogenic strains, not nonpathogenic strains.
  2. Inactivating the associated gene should measurably reduce pathogenicity or virulence.
  3. Reversing the mutation or replacing the gene with the wild type should restore pathogenicity or virulence.
Key Connection
Classic Koch’s postulates track the organism → disease relationship. Molecular Koch’s postulates track the virulence gene → disease property relationship.
Understand It Better: molecular guidelines for microbial disease causation
  1. A putative pathogen’s nucleic-acid sequence should be present in most cases, preferably at sites where pathology is evident.
  2. It should be absent from most healthy controls; when detected, it should occur at lower prevalence and in lower copy numbers than in disease.
  3. The copy number should fall or become undetectable when disease resolves, and rise with relapse or recurrence.
  4. Detection in healthy subjects should help predict subsequent development of disease.
  5. The organism inferred from the sequence should fit known biologic characteristics of related organisms and the nature of the disease; significance increases when genotype predicts morphology, pathology, clinical features, and host response.

4Clinical diseaseManifestations may themselves become a source for further transmission.

Genomic basis of pathogenicity

Bacterial virulence is partly a genetics story: genes that encode toxins, capsules, adherence, invasion, or resistance may move between DNA locations or be acquired as larger blocks.

PDF pp. 1–2

Plasmids

Small, double-stranded, helical, non-chromosomal DNA molecules.

Why they matter: the lecture lists plasmid-encoded enterotoxins, hemolysin, adherence/invasion products, and the two virulence plasmids of B. anthracis.

Transposons

Small DNA pieces that encode enzymes allowing movement from one DNA location to another, either on the same DNA molecule or a different molecule.

Key idea: they relocate genetic information.

Bacteriophages

The lecture identifies phages as mobile genetic elements and illustrates a viral genome entering a bacterial cell.

Lecture examples: genes for botulinum, diphtheria, and cholera toxins may be phage encoded.

CarrierOrganismEncoded virulence factor and disease role
PlasmidE. coliHeat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins causing diarrhea; hemolysin associated with invasive disease and urinary tract infections
E. coli and ShigellaAdherence factors and products involved in mucosal invasion
B. anthracisCapsule essential for virulence on one plasmid
B. anthracisEdema factor, lethal factor, and protective antigen on another plasmid
PhageC. botulinumBotulinum toxin causing paralysis
Corynebacterium diphtheriaeDiphtheria toxin inhibiting human protein synthesis
V. choleraeCholera toxin causing severe watery diarrhea

Pathogenicity islands

What they are

Pathogenicity islands (PAIs) are large groups of genes associated with pathogenicity and located on the bacterial chromosome. They are distinct genetic elements encoding virulence factors and belong to the wider class of genomic islands.

Genomic islands are acquired by horizontal gene transfer. By promoting genetic variability, they contribute to microbial evolution.

How selection works

  1. Transferred DNA is acquired and/or genetic material is deleted.
  2. A genomic island is selected.
  3. If its gene products improve recipient fitness, island-harboring bacteria are positively selected.
  4. The foreign DNA block may support environmental survival, saprophytic life, symbiosis, or pathogenicity.
E. coli as the lecture’s example
Some E. coli strains became pathogenic by acquiring virulence factors through plasmids, transposons, bacteriophages, and/or pathogenicity islands. The lecture says pathogenic intestinal strains are classified into four groups and lists EHEC/VTEC, ETEC, EPEC, and “EIEC or EAEC” on the fourth line.

Adherence and invasion

Once bacteria enter the body, they must remain at a useful site and, for invasive organisms, cross into host cells or tissues.

PDF pp. 2–3
Core Idea
Adherence comes before stable colonization. Bacteria use specific surface molecules to interact with host cells; the lecture then shows how attachment can progress from a first contact to intimate attachment and colonization.

Pili

Thick, rod-like appendages. Although the lecture notes a role in movement, it emphasizes their more frequent role in adherence to surfaces, which facilitates infection.

Initial contactIntimate attachmentColonization

Fimbriae

Hairlike appendages extending from the cell surface.

The lecture’s example is the fimbriae of Streptococcus pyogenes, which contain M protein.

AInitial attachmentFree-floating bacteria extend pili toward the apical host-cell surface; a tip protein may participate.
BIntimate attachmentAncillary pilus proteins may form zipper-like adhesion and reduce the distance between bacterial and host surfaces.
CColonizationHigh-affinity surface adhesins mediate colonization of the apical surface.
DCommunity and inflammationPilus-mediated aggregation supports microbial community formation; increased density may increase innate response and inflammation.

Invasion of host cells and tissues

What invasion means

The lecture uses invasion to mean the entry of bacteria into host cells.

This differs from adherence: attachment keeps the organism in contact with the surface; invasion moves it into the cell.

Listeria monocytogenes

  1. Induces engulfment by host cells.
  2. Uses actin for movement within a cell.
  3. Also requires actin for movement between cells.

What happens next: the organism can progress through an intracellular life cycle rather than remaining only on the surface.

Lock It In
Core conceptAttachment anchors; invasion enters.
DifferentiatorPili are thick/rod-like; fimbriae are hairlike.
Key sequenceInitial attachment → intimate attachment → colonization.
Exam cueListeria movement within and between cells requires actin.

Exotoxins and endotoxins

The major distinction is whether the toxin is a secreted protein or a structural component associated with the Gram-negative outer membrane.

PDF pp. 3–5

Exotoxin

Diffusible protein secreted into the surrounding medium, produced by both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.

In the lecture, enterotoxins are grouped under secreted toxins.

VS

Endotoxin

Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria; classic endotoxin is liberated with bacterial lysis, and the table notes release may also occur during growth.

FeatureExotoxinsEndotoxins (LPS)
Source/releaseExcreted by living cells; high concentration in liquid mediumIntegral part of Gram-negative cell wall; released on death and partly during growth; may not need release for biologic activity
Which bacteriaBoth Gram-positive and Gram-negativeGram-negative only
NaturePolypeptides, molecular weight 10,000–900,000LPS complexes; lipid A probably responsible for toxicity
Heat stabilityRelatively unstable; toxicity often destroyed rapidly above 60°CRelatively stable; withstands heating above 60°C for hours without loss of toxicity
Immune responseHighly antigenic; high-titer antitoxin; antitoxin neutralizes toxinWeakly immunogenic; antibodies may be antitoxic/protective, but antibody titer–protection relationship is less clear
Toxoid formationCan be converted to antigenic, nontoxic toxoids by formalin, acid, heat, etc.; toxoids used for immunizationNot converted to toxoids
Relative toxicityHighly toxic; fatal in microgram quantities or lessModerately toxic; fatal in tens to hundreds of micrograms
ReceptorsUsually bind specific cell receptorsSpecific receptors not found on cells
FeverUsually do not produce feverUsually produce fever through IL-1 and other mediators
Genetic controlFrequently extrachromosomal, such as plasmidsSynthesis directed by chromosomal genes

1LPS enters bloodstreamInitially binds circulating proteins.
2Cell interactionInteracts with macrophages, neutrophils, and other reticuloendothelial cells.
3Mediator releaseIL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF, and other cytokines are released.
4Cascades activateComplement and coagulation cascades are activated.

The lecture states that Gram-positive peptidoglycan has the same biologic activities as LPS, but is much less potent.

The uploaded trans does not resolve this conflict; this reviewer therefore flags it rather than presenting the answer-key classification as settled.
Lock It In

DifferentiatorToxoids can be made from exotoxins, not endotoxins.

Toxin examples and downstream effects

The lecture’s toxin examples are best remembered by following the molecular action to the final clinical or cellular effect.

PDF pp. 4–5

Diphtheria toxin

1Secreted exotoxinC. diphtheriae secretes the toxin.
2Receptor binding and entryThe exotoxin binds a host-cell surface receptor and enters the cell.
3EF-2 inactivationThe toxin inactivates elongation factor 2.
4Protein synthesis stopsRibosomes cannot continue protein synthesis.
5Cell deathDeath of multiple throat cells forms the characteristic gray pseudomembrane.

Botulinum toxin

The lecture states that botulinum toxin produces flaccid paralysis and stops muscle contraction.

The diagram shows the toxin blocking release of acetylcholine from the axon terminal, preventing contraction.

Tetanus toxin

The lecture states that tetanus toxin produces spastic paralysis.

The diagrams show blockade of inhibitory transmitter release, specifically glycine and GABA, followed by continuous excitatory stimulation.

Cholera toxin

1Small-intestinal colonizationV. cholerae colonizes the small intestine.
2Toxin releaseThe bacterium releases toxins.
3Continuous channel activationElectrolyte channels remain activated.
4Electrolytes move to lumenElectrolytes are pushed from cells into the intestinal lumen.
5Watery outputThe lecture links this to “rice-water” stools.

Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning and emesis

Lecture statements

  • S. aureus releases MSCRAMM (microbial surface component recognizing adhesive matrix molecule), composed of several protein types.
  • The toxin induces vomiting.
  • Potential food sources and toxin formation are shown in the lecture’s overview figure.

Enterotoxin-induced emesis

  1. Enterotoxins cross through mucus-expelling goblet cells and epithelial cells.
  2. They reach the lamina propria.
  3. They interact with mast cells, causing release of 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT).
  4. 5-HT interacts with the vagus nerve.
  5. An emetic response follows.

The lecture also names T cells and neutrophils as possible additional targets.

Lock It In
Core conceptTrack toxin action to its final host effect.
DifferentiatorBotulinum = flaccid; tetanus = spastic.
Key sequenceDiphtheria toxin → EF-2 → no protein synthesis.
Exam cueRice-water stool points to the lecture’s V. cholerae toxin pathway.

Enzymes and tissue spread

Unlike toxins, these enzymes are described as not intrinsically toxic. Their importance lies in changing tissue barriers, membranes, extracellular material, or antibodies in ways that assist infection.

PDF pp. 5–6
Core Idea
Enzymes create access. They can dissolve material that holds cells together, remove DNA traps, damage membranes, break collagen, or split IgA1.
ClassLecture exampleTarget and result
GlycohydrolasesHyaluronidase S in S. aureusDegrades hyaluronic acid that cements cells together, promoting spread through tissue
NucleasesDNase produced by S. aureusDegrades DNA from dying bacterial and host cells that can trap bacteria, thereby promoting spread
PhospholipasesPhospholipase C of B. anthracisDegrades the host phospholipid bilayer, causing cellular lysis; also degrades phagosomal membranes to allow cytoplasmic escape
ProteasesCollagenase in C. perfringensDegrades collagen in connective tissue to promote spread

Clostridium perfringens

The lecture highlights lecithinase and collagenase.

In the blood-vessel diagram, collagenase breaks collagen between endothelial cells. Breakdown of collagen and endothelium allows bacteria to enter the bloodstream and be carried throughout the body.

Hyaluronidase

Hyaluronan is shown as a polymer connecting adjacent cells in epidermal layers.

Hyaluronidase degrades this adhesive extracellular-matrix polymer, creating a passage between cells that would otherwise be blocked.

IgA1 proteases

What they do

IgA1 proteases split IgA1, the primary form of IgA named in the lecture, thereby inactivating its antibody activity.

Lecture examples

  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae
  • Neisseria meningitidis
  • Haemophilus influenzae
Internal Layout Note
The line “same biologic activities as LPS, but much less potent than LPS” appears under both Gram-positive peptidoglycan and the following tissue-degrading enzymes heading. The enzyme table itself instead describes specific tissue-spreading functions. The trans does not explain the repeated line, so this reviewer does not treat it as a general property of the enzymes.
Lock It In
Core conceptEnzymes facilitate infection without being intrinsically toxic.
DifferentiatorHyaluronidase breaks matrix; collagenase breaks collagen; IgA1 protease breaks antibody.
Key sequenceBarrier degradation → tissue passage → possible bloodstream access.
Exam cueDNase removes extracellular DNA that can trap bacteria.

Antiphagocytic factors and intracellular survival

Some virulence factors prevent phagocytosis; others allow survival after the bacterium has already been taken up.

PDF pp. 6–7

Antiphagocytic capsule

A polysaccharide capsule protects bacteria from macrophages and other phagocytic cells.

Lecture examples: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis.

→

Intracellular pathogenicity

The bacterium is taken up but alters the intracellular pathway so it can survive and grow.

Lecture example: Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis: step-by-step survival

1Macrophage uptakeBacteria enter a phagosome.
2Fusion is blockedThe M. tuberculosis–containing phagosome cannot fuse with lysosomes or mature.
3Growth continuesThe failure of maturation permits bacterial survival and growth.
4Ca²⁺ fallsCa²⁺-dependent pathways decrease, including production of bactericidal ROS/RNS.
5Cytokine balance shiftsExcess IL-10 limits IL-12, which limits IFN production by T cells.
Lock It In
Core conceptA capsule prevents uptake; M. tuberculosis survives after uptake.
DifferentiatorExtracellular shield vs intracellular pathway disruption.
Key sequencePhagosome uptake → no lysosomal fusion → survival/growth.
Exam cueExcess IL-10 limits IL-12 and then T-cell IFN production.

Antigenic heterogeneity and gonococcal immune evasion

The lecture uses Neisseria gonorrhoeae to show that immune evasion can occur at several levels: complement, phagocytes, dendritic cells, T cells, and the bacterium’s own changing surface.

PDF p. 7
Simple Idea
Gonococci frequently switch from one antigenic form to another. By changing what is displayed on the surface, they make stable immune recognition more difficult.

A. Complement evasion

  • Binds complement proteins to prevent opsonization and membrane-attack-complex killing.
  • Sialylates LOS to hide from complement.
  • Binds factor H and C4b-binding protein, presenting as self and shielding itself.
  • Binds CR3 and the iC3b receptor, a process thought to assist epithelial invasion.

B. Phagocytes and dendritic cells

  • Survives in and around macrophages and neutrophils.
  • Survives inside macrophage phagosomes and modulates apoptosis and inflammatory cytokines.
  • Polarizes macrophages so they are less able to activate T cells.
  • Dendritic cells exposed to the organism stimulate less T-cell proliferation.

C. Adaptive immune modulation

  • Infection does not generate immunological memory in the lecture’s description.
  • Surface structures undergo antigenic and phase variation: type IV pili, Opa proteins, and LOS.
  • TH1 and TH2 proliferation and activation are suppressed through effects on cytokine production.
Key Connection
Antigenic heterogeneity is not presented as a single isolated trick. It combines with complement binding, intracellular survival, and immune-cell modulation to create a broader immune-evasion strategy.
Lock It In
Core conceptFrequent surface change helps gonococci elude immunity.
DifferentiatorAntigenic/phase variation affects type IV pili, Opa, and LOS.
Key sequenceComplement evasion + phagocyte survival + reduced T-cell activation.
Exam cueFactor H and C4BP binding supports serum resistance in the lecture.

Bacterial secretion systems

Secretion systems are transport routes that move bacterial proteins—or, in some type 4 examples, DNA—into another bacterial compartment, the environment, or a host context where they participate in pathogenesis.

PDF pp. 7–8

General Sec pathway

Both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria use a general Sec pathway as a major protein-secretion mechanism.

  • Participates in insertion of bacterial membrane proteins.
  • Serves as the major route for most proteins crossing the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane.

Sec dependence

The lecture describes Type 2 as using Sec to first move proteins to the periplasm, then an outer-membrane pore complex completes secretion. Cholera toxin is a listed example.

The summary bullets label Type 5 as Sec dependent and Types 1, 3, 4, and 6 as Sec independent; the detailed table describes Type 4 as both Sec dependent and Sec independent.

SystemRoute in lectureOrganisms and substrates/roles listed
Type 1Sec-independentE. coli α-hemolysin; Proteus vulgaris and Morganella morganii hemolysin; B. pertussis adenylate cyclase producing cAMP; P. aeruginosa alkaline protease; S. marcescens Zn protease causing host-cell damage
Type 2Sec-dependentP. aeruginosa elastase, exotoxin A, phospholipase C; L. pneumophila acid phosphatase, lipase, phospholipase, protease, RNase; V. cholerae cholera toxin; S. marcescens hemolysin
Type 3Sec-independent; contact-dependentYersinia Ysc-Yop blocks phagocytosis and induces apoptosis; P. aeruginosa cytotoxin; Shigella controls host signaling, invasion, death; Salmonella enterica SPI1/SPI2 effectors promote attachment and invasion; E. coli direct cytotoxicity; V. parahaemolyticus is listed without a role in the table
Type 4Sec-dependent and Sec-independentProtein substrates: B. pertussis pertussis toxin; H. pylori cytotoxin. DNA substrates: N. gonorrhoeae DNA export; H. pylori DNA uptake and release
Type 5Sec-dependentN. gonorrhoeae IgA1 protease; H. influenzae IgA1 protease and adhesins; E. coli serine protease, adhesins, type 1 pili, P-pili; Shigella flexneri serine protease; S. marcescens proteases; Bordetella adhesins; B. pertussis filamentous hemagglutinin; Y. pestis capsular antigen

The lecture explicitly says there is no need to memorize all secretion systems. The goal is to understand that these systems participate in pathogenesis by delivering particular bacterial products.

DifferentiatorType 3 is contact-dependent; Type 4 can move protein or DNA.

Common exam traps from the lecture

  • Diphtheria toxin inhibits EF-2, not a pore-forming mechanism.
  • Exotoxins are not limited to Gram-negative bacteria; the lecture states both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms can produce them.
  • Cholera toxin is secreted, not attached to the flagellum.
  • Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 is listed under S. aureus, not S. epidermidis.
  • LPS is part of the Gram-negative cell wall/outer membrane.

Trans issues to remember

  • Infectious dose appears in the outline but has no developed section.
  • The lecture says “four” pathogenic intestinal E. coli groups but pairs EIEC/EAEC in one item.
  • The review key’s heat-stable-enterotoxin classification conflicts with the earlier framework.
  • A repeated LPS/peptidoglycan sentence appears under tissue-degrading enzymes.
  • A Type 3 secretion-system row is visually misaligned.
Lock It In
Core conceptCompare by function, location, and sequence.
Main differentiatorAsk: attached, secreted, structural, degradative, or evasive?
Key sequenceGenetic acquisition → virulence factor → host effect.

Cram Sheet

Rapid retrieval of the lecture’s definitions, mechanisms, distinctions, and exam cues. No new content is introduced here.

PDF pp. 1–8

Causation

  • Koch: present in cases → pure culture → disease in susceptible animal → re-isolate.
  • Molecular Koch: virulence phenotype associated → gene inactivation reduces virulence → gene restoration restores it.
  • Nucleic-acid guidelines: more common/higher copy in disease, falls with resolution, may predict later disease.

Transmission

  • Animal food sources: Salmonella, Campylobacter.
  • Inadvertent severe infection: Y. pestis, B. anthracis.
  • Manifestations spread organisms: cholera stool, sewage-associated E. coli, nasal S. aureus.

Genomic virulence

  • Plasmid: small, ds, helical, non-chromosomal DNA.
  • Transposon: mobile DNA piece encoding movement enzymes.
  • Phage-encoded toxins: botulinum, diphtheria, cholera.
  • PAI: large chromosomal virulence-gene cluster acquired through horizontal transfer.

Adherence & invasion

  • Pili: thick rod-like; initial → intimate → colonization.
  • Fimbriae: hairlike; S. pyogenes example contains M protein.
  • Invasion: entry into host cells.
  • Listeria: engulfment plus actin-based intracellular/intercellular movement.

Exotoxin vs endotoxin

  • Exotoxin: secreted protein, both Gram types, often heat-labile, highly antigenic, toxoid possible, usually specific receptor, usually no fever.
  • Endotoxin: Gram-negative LPS, lipid A toxicity, heat-stable, weakly immunogenic, no toxoid, usually fever, chromosomal synthesis.

Toxin mechanisms

  • Diphtheria: EF-2 inactivation → no protein synthesis → cell death → gray pseudomembrane.
  • Botulinum: blocks acetylcholine release → flaccid paralysis.
  • Tetanus: blocks glycine/GABA release → continuous excitation → spastic paralysis.
  • Cholera: continuous electrolyte-channel activation → lumen electrolyte movement → rice-water stool.

LPS pathway

LPS in blood → circulating-protein binding → macrophage/neutrophil interaction → IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF → complement/coagulation → fever, leukopenia, hypotension, DIC.

Gram-positive peptidoglycan: same biologic activities in the lecture, but much less potent.

Enzymes

  • Hyaluronidase: hyaluronic acid/hyaluronan → tissue passage.
  • DNase: extracellular DNA traps → spread.
  • Phospholipase C: host and phagosomal membrane damage.
  • Collagenase: collagen → connective-tissue/endothelial spread.
  • IgA1 protease: splits IgA1, inactivating antibody activity.

Persistence & evasion

  • Capsule: protects S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis from phagocytes.
  • M. tuberculosis: blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion, lowers Ca²⁺-dependent ROS/RNS, excess IL-10 limits IL-12 and IFN.
  • N. gonorrhoeae: complement binding, phagosome survival, reduced T-cell activation, antigenic/phase variation of pili, Opa, LOS.

Secretion systems

  • Sec: major route across cytoplasmic membrane.
  • Type 2: Sec → periplasm → outer-membrane channel; cholera toxin example.
  • Type 3: Sec-independent, contact-dependent.
  • Type 4: protein or DNA substrates.
  • Type 5: IgA1 protease among examples.
  • Type 7: M. tuberculosis CFP-10/ESAT-6.

If you see X, think Y

  • EF-2 inhibition → diphtheria toxin.
  • Rice-water stool → lecture’s cholera toxin pathway.
  • Flaccid vs spastic → botulinum vs tetanus.
  • Fever + LPS → IL-1/other mediators and systemic cascade.
  • Actin-based cell-to-cell movement → Listeria.
  • No phagosome-lysosome fusion → M. tuberculosis.

Lecture cautions
